blocks: The Brief already says budgets come from measurement on the encode garden. Frontier performance adds targets in the same terms: a warm garden page resolve finishes in about the time git status takes in this repository, editor completion returns before the next keystroke lands, and a cold parse of the encode garden is paid about once per checkout. Codex's benchmark rows measure all of those. The rows for repeated short-lived processes and for completion during a background parse are the ones that catch a tool that is fast in a demo and slow in a session.

Codex's Person/codekiln/GitHub/logseq-gardener/Analysis/Codex/26/09/12/0733 ET Resolve pages through evidence from the whole graph is right, and it corrects my Person/codekiln/GitHub/logseq-gardener/Analysis/Fable/26/09/12/0658 ET Ship the agent CLI first and let the LSP inherit the index: a page-existence command that reads only pages/ would say that CLI does not exist, while the Goals page links it. In a Logseq file graph a name exists when a file carries it, when a title:: property declares it, when another page declares it as an alias::, when any block links or tags it, or when it is an ancestor inside a namespaced name. Logseq's extract code in extract.cljc builds pages from all of those sources at once, and the tool should too.

The resolver returns one of a fixed set of results, so a caller cannot read an ambiguous or provisional answer as a plain match. My/Principle/Make Illegal States Unrepresentable is the reason, and My/Principle/Dispel Ambiguity is what the caller gets from it.
Answer page existence with a typed result and an exit code

A fuzzy suggestion lives only inside NoMatch, so punctuation normalization can never silently resolve a misspelling to a different page. When two pages declare the same alias::, the resolver lists both of them in the evidence and answers Ambiguous.

This garden's logseq/config.edn sets :file/name-format :triple-lowbar and :journal/page-title-format "yyyy-MM-dd EEE". The name format turns Person___codekiln.md into Person/codekiln, and the title format turns journals/2026_09_12.md into 2026-09-12 Sat. Change either setting and the same files name different pages, so the resolver loads the configuration before it names anything, and the cache key includes it.

It exercises block matching on real edits before the merge driver in Person/codekiln/GitHub/logseq-gardener/Analysis/Fable/26/09/12/0658 ET A Logseq-aware git merge driver before a CRDT trusts that matching. git diff shows the lines an edit changed. This command shows the links, targets, parents, and block identities an edit changed, over the same --base <revision> argument, so garden diff says what it is to anyone who has used git, and garden diff --base HEAD reads as the graph counterpart of git diff HEAD. "Impact" names a consequence of the output, and "diff" names the output.
Call the impact command garden diff and run it where the link checker runs
Name it after what it does

The name also fits the integration git offers. .gitattributes can name an external diff driver for pages/*.md and journals/*.md (gitattributes, Defining an external diff driver), so git diff on a garden file can show the graph changes beside the text changes when a person asks for that view. Registering the merge driver later takes one more line in .gitattributes, described in gitattributes, Defining a custom merge driver on that same page. My/Principle/Simplify/Prefer Standards and Defaults applies.

This repository runs resolve-wikilinks.cljs from the link-hygiene skill when an agent drafts a page, and lefthook runs the identity scan on every commit. garden diff --base HEAD --json in those places reports new fileless pages, links whose target changed, blocks whose parent changed, and removed id:: lines that other blocks still reference. The report on new fileless pages does what resolve-wikilinks.cljs does today, so garden diff replaces it. The reports on changed link targets, changed block parents and removed id:: lines are checks this repository has never had.

Codex's rule stands: match blocks by explicit UUID when present, and report an ID-less match as uncertain when repeated text makes it so. The diff needs a two-way match between base and current, and the merge driver needs a three-way match among base, ours, and theirs. Write the matcher once with three inputs in mind, and the diff becomes its first user and its test bed.

So the first publisher must expand page and block embeds, resolve block references, and render the YouTube and video macros. It can leave every query as its source text with a visible note, and on this corpus that touches the three files in the table. Publishing before query evaluation, which the Brief schedules and Codex questions, costs almost nothing here. {{cards}} selects blocks by a query, so the report counts it with the queries.

codekiln asked on the pull request how the Frontmatter page is assembled from subpages. The body of Logseq/Frontmatter is a list of {{embed [[Logseq/Frontmatter/tags]]}} lines and their siblings, so a publisher that copies the file's text renders a page of macro syntax, and a publisher that expands embeds renders the conventions. That page is the first fixture for the embed expander.

Codex asks the build to record which pages include text from other pages, so that editing an included block rebuilds the pages that show it. garden diff reads the same index to list the pages a block edit reaches, and the merge driver reads it to tell whether two branches changed the same block. Build the inclusion index once in garden-core, and let the publisher, garden diff, and the merge driver all read it.

Codex's Person/codekiln/GitHub/logseq-gardener/Analysis/Codex/26/09/12/0733 ET Keep editor buffers and worktrees separate in the shared cache names a boundary the Brief leaves out: the saved files, an unsaved Neovim buffer, and an agent's worktree can hold different text for the same path. The editor half of the argument is right and is standard practice. The worktree half can be simpler than Codex proposes.
Give each checkout its own cache and share parsed text later
The editor keeps an overlay of open buffers
Give each checkout its own cache and share parsed text later

The LSP client sends the text of every open document, and that text wins over the file on disk until the document closes. rust-analyzer and other language servers keep those buffers as an overlay on top of a snapshot of the disk, and garden-core should take the same shape: a source of files that is either the checkout on disk or the checkout with an overlay of open buffers on top.
Give each checkout its own cache and share parsed text later

A parse result that arrives for an older version of a buffer is discarded, as Codex says.

Codex proposes sharing parsed content between worktrees, keyed by content hash, while keeping file membership and reference indexes per checkout. I would leave the sharing out of the first version. Key the cache by the real path of the directory that holds logseq/config.edn, store it under $XDG_CACHE_HOME/<tool>/<hash of that path>/, and let each worktree pay one cold parse when it is created.

Worktrees in this repository live for one pull request, per My/Pref/Dev/Tool/git/Worktree, so a per-worktree cold parse happens about as often as git worktree add does. A shared content store is a second index with its own eviction rules, and My/Principle/Simplify/Minimize Surface Area says to leave it out until a worktree's first command is slow enough that someone notices. Use Logseq's own graph-parser as the oracle and require a byte-identical round trip

Codex's Person/codekiln/GitHub/logseq-gardener/Analysis/Codex/26/09/12/0733 ET Test graph meaning and preserve the original source text adds two tests to the parser decision in Person/codekiln/GitHub/logseq-gardener/Analysis/Fable/26/09/12/0658 ET Pick the parser first and let the language follow: compare the graph the tool builds with the graph Logseq builds, and keep the original text so a later edit changes only the bytes it means to. Both tests are right, and both can run this week with tools already on this machine. Logseq's graph-parser is the reference answer: whatever it says a graph contains is what the new tool has to match.
Use Logseq's own graph-parser as the oracle and require a byte-identical round trip
Logseq's own parser can produce the answers to compare against

codekiln asked on the Codex page what a second comparison after syntax parsing means. lsdoc's test checks one file at a time: does lsdoc read this file into the same blocks and inline nodes that mldoc does. The second check reads the whole graph: does the new tool name the same pages, join the same aliases, give each block the same parent, and find the same backlinks that Logseq finds. Logseq computes those in ClojureScript after mldoc has parsed, so lsdoc's test never runs that code.
Use Logseq's own graph-parser as the oracle and require a byte-identical round trip
Logseq's own parser can produce the answers to compare against

lsdoc's differential test compares its syntax tree with mldoc's on a normalized projection of blocks, inline nodes, and references, and its README says spans are excluded from that comparison (lsdoc README, The oracle). Page naming, alias and tag extraction, journal conversion, block order, and duplicate-ID handling sit above that tree, in Logseq's extract.cljc, so the differential test says nothing about them.
Use Logseq's own graph-parser as the oracle and require a byte-identical round trip
Logseq's own parser can produce the answers to compare against

nbb-logseq is installed here through mise, the link-hygiene and flashcard skills already run ClojureScript scripts under it, and its README says the graph-parser's namespaces all load under it (nbb-logseq README). A short script can therefore run Logseq's own extract over the encode garden and write pages, aliases, tags, block parents, references, and explicit UUIDs to JSON. Check out logseq/logseq at the tag 0.10.15, the release codekiln's Brewfile pins the desktop app to, so the oracle and the app a person opens the garden in agree. That JSON file is the golden fixture the new tool's output is compared with, page by page, with the tag recorded beside it. Run the same dump over logseq/docs, the public Logseq graph cloned at ~/ghq/github.com/logseq/docs, so the comparison also covers a graph codekiln did not write, which the Brief asks for.

The round trip is a pass-or-fail test

Parse every file in the encode garden and in logseq/docs, serialize each back, and require identical bytes. A parser that passes can support small edits. A parser that fails needs a separate layer that keeps original text and spans, which is what Codex describes. Tine's README says tine-core's tests include a parse/serialize round trip, that round-trip parsing is validated against a real Logseq graph, and that tine-check proves byte-faithful serialization without reading note content (Tine README, Testing). Running tine-check on the encode garden is the cheapest way to learn whether that claim holds for this corpus.

The round trip is a pass-or-fail test

Files the round trip cannot reproduce are findings. Each one is either a construct the parser should learn or a file this garden should fix, and the list of them is the compatibility report the Brief asks for.

Rust when all three tests pass, OCaml when the syntax test fails

Rust on lsdoc and tine-core stays the path when lsdoc's differential test, the graph-parser comparison, and the byte round trip all pass on the encode garden. A failure in the graph comparison points at extract code the new tool must port; a failure in the round trip points at the serializer. OCaml on mldoc remains the fallback when the syntax comparison itself fails, and since Logseq's graph layer is ClojureScript, that path ports extract as well.
